source: Royal Government of Cambodia, General Directorate of Agriculture (GDA) / Boosting Food Production Program (PMO), "ខែ្សសង្វាក់ផលិតកម្ម ដំណាំពោតនៅកម្ពុជា" (Corn Production Value Chain in Cambodia), 2017
text:
When asked about problems they expect to face growing red corn going forward, the 250 surveyed households ranked the following challenges by how often each was cited: increasing weed pressure (221 households, 88% of respondents); increasing insect/pest damage to the crop (159, 64%); soil becoming harder/more compacted (146, 58%); soil losing fertility due to erosion/washing away (143, 57%); natural disasters or unpredictable rainfall (122, 49%); declining yields (120, 48%); increasing yields (a positive expectation cited by 47 households, 19%); crop disease (33, 13%); rising seed prices (22, 9%); poor seed quality (3, 1%); and 38 households (15%) said they were not aware of any particular problem.

When the top six of these concerns were further ranked by severity (high/medium/low) among households that raised them: weed pressure was rated high-severity by 56 households, medium by 24, low by 8 (88 total); pest damage was rated high by 23, medium by 27, low by 14 (64 total); soil hardening was rated high by 24, medium by 26, low by 8 (58 total); soil fertility loss was rated high by 20, medium by 27, low by 10 (57 total); yield decline was rated high by 16, medium by 18, low by 14 (48 total); and yield increase (positive) was rated high by 2, medium by 12, low by 6 (19 total).

The document interprets this as showing farmers attribute declining yield largely to soil degradation from continuous cultivation, and that improved seed quality alone would not solve declining productivity without addressing soil health and weed/pest pressure.
